newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - US oil refiners brace for air war with EPA.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - US oil refiners brace for air war with EPA.

text.p: U.S. oil refiners, still recovering from environmental costs related to the Clean Air Act, are bracing to fight U.S. regulators this year over an ambitious proposal that would raise air quality even more.
The proposal points to wider use of clean-burning motor fuels, thus provoking resistance from refiners who have traced poor profits this decade in part to environmental expenses.
"We think that the refining industry would be one of the most adversely impacted," said Urvin Sternfels, head of the National Petroleum Refiners Association (NPRA), a trade group.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposal, made public late last year, would toughen the threshold for acceptable levels of smog, and would also target much smaller dust particles, called particulates.

The proposal, regarded as the most complex air regulations ever, would affect the way refiners, manufacturers and coal-burning power generators do business, though none will be affected until at least the year 2000.

Refiners' costs to meet the new standards would run in the billions according to Sternfels, adding to the $37 billion the industry is already expected to spend between 1990 and 2002 to meet existing requirements in the Clean Air Act of 1990.
While economics will surely be a key topic in discussions of the EPA's plan, public health advocates and environmentalists are expected to mount a vigorous argument that the costs are warranted.
Armed with studies they say suggest current standards are inadequate to protect the public and in some cases are not being met, health advocates appear poised for battle.

"Not only does the law require reassessing standards, it's also the right thing to do," said Jason Grumet, executive director of Northeast States for Coordinated Air Use Management, an air quality group in the populous Northeast.

Still, industry and public policy sources predict discussions on the proposal, which will begin later this month and are set to wrap up by June, are likely to be held in a spirit of compromise and cooperation.

They say the re-election of Democratic president Bill Clinton and a re-elected Republican majority in Congress seen less hostile to environmental causes, should ensure EPA's proposal a thorough, if heated, hearing.
"The indication right now is that Congress is concerned about this, but I don't see a knee-jerk reaction against it," said Paul Bailey of the American Petroleum Institute (API).
"Right now, using scientific and economic jusifications, we are trying to convince the EPA there is no reason for changing either of these standards," said API's Bailey.
Both API and the NPRA are arguing that more data ought to be collected before the government starts asking industry to again invest heavily in efforts to clean the air.

They say connections between smog and a troubling asthma problem in big cities have not been clearly established, nor have claims that small particulate emissions are related to premature death and to sundry health problems.
To advocacy groups on the other side of the divide, those claims are nothing more than hot air.

"It's kind of like the tobacco industry denying the danger of cigarettes even after countless studies," said Diane Maple, spokeswoman for the American Lung Association in Washington, D.C., referring to the calls for more studies. "How many more studies do you need?"
At least one air scientist, S.T. Rao at the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), agrees the data collected is probably the most comprehensive ever.
"This is the first time a comprehensive and credible database has been looked at," said Rao, who heads the DEC's Bureau of Air Research.

Rao said the proposal, by expanding pollution controls across different states and industries, will further the notion that air quality is a long-term and interstate challenge rather than just a parochial one.
Some analysts said the EPA is biting off more than it can chew politically, and EPA officials acknowledge the proposal is just that -- a proposal.

"I'm not sure the final rule will look like the proposal," said Dave Ryan, a spokesman at EPA's Washington D.C headquarters. "But whatever happens, we don't don't expect any real world impact until at least the year 2000."

Oil industry analysts and consultants meanwhile say for refiners, California is again the benchmarch against which the rest of the country must define its progress in the battle for cleaner air. The Los Angeles area has the worst smog problem in the country, but its clean fuels are helping, sources said.
"We're going to eventually end up with a diesel fuel that looks very much like the one in California," said George Unzelman, president of HyOx Inc, a California-based clean fuels consultancy.
California's diesel burns much more cleanly than the low sulphur diesel required outside the state since 1993.

Unzelman also speculated that eventually the new EPA proposal could hasten the nationwide use of a gasoline as clean-burning as the one now required in California. Under current laws, such clean-burning gasolines would only be required in big cities outside of California from next year.
Sources note that cleaner-burning diesel and gasoline alike would help fight both smog and particulates.

"Maybe it all doesn't have to be done right now from a public policy point of view. But it will have to be done sooner or later. We continue to put people on this planet and we continue to drive more and more cars," Unzelman said.
